description:
The Shrine of Hazrat Shah Ali Akbar Shamsi stands in the historic neighbourhood of Suraj Miani in Multan, the celebrated "city of saints", and is counted among the oldest and most beautiful mausoleums of the city. Shah Ali Akbar is remembered as a descendant — by tradition of the eighth generation — of the great Sufi Shah Shams Sabzwari of Multan, and it is said that after the death of his father he settled permanently in the city. His tomb, built of brick in the octagonal, tiered form so characteristic of Multan, is often likened to a smaller version of the famous shrine of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, and it belongs to the classic tradition of Multani funerary architecture with its glazed tilework and tapering silhouette. According to inscriptions and local tradition, construction of the mausoleum began in 993 AH (about 1585 CE) and took some fifteen years to complete; it is said to have been raised by the saint's grandson, who is himself buried within the complex, and the work is attributed to the builders Ibrahim and Rajab, sons of the noted architect Musa Lahori. Despite its remarkable beauty and its importance to the architectural history of Multan, the shrine has often been described as one of the city's more neglected monuments. It remains a place of *ziyarat* and hosts an annual *urs* in the saint's honour. Also known by the alternate name Kabuli Mohallah, the shrine's compound is registered as a protected monument under the Antiquity Act of 1975 by the Directorate General of Archaeology, Punjab, whose own listing describes the building's brick construction as embellished with panels of glazed tiles, three arched panels on each side surmounted by a series of merlons set on bold moldings, its lower walls plastered in lime, and an interior decorated with panels of fresco painting — though the same listing notes this fresco work and lime plaster have been considerably damaged by the smoke of mustard-oil lamps and votive candles over the years. In 2019 the Punjab Archaeology Department proposed a Rs 30 million conservation and restoration project for the mausoleum, and by November of that year a related tender for a Rs 27.104 million project was opened for bids, though press reporting does not clarify whether this represents the same project re-costed or a later phase of the work.

## Bibliography
- Sana Jamal and Imran Adnan, "Bids for conservation of tomb to open on November 18," *The Express Tribune*, 5 November 2019.
- "Govt approves Rs30m to restore historic Multan site," *The Express Tribune*, 21 May 2019.
- Directorate General of Archaeology, Government of Punjab, "Tomb of Shah Ali Akbar & His Mother, Multan," https://archaeology.punjab.gov.pk/tomb_shahaliakbar, accessed 16 August 2026.
qa_note: Two Express Tribune articles (21 May 2019 and 5 November 2019) and the Punjab Archaeology Department's own official page were all directly verified, but the press pieces conflict with the official custodial body on two central facts, neither resolved here. Construction date: The Express Tribune (both 2019 articles) states the mausoleum "was built in 1585"; the Directorate General of Archaeology, Punjab's own official listing for the same monument instead states "it may be attributed to the 17th century A.D." Founder's identity and lineage: press names the saint "Hazrat Shah Ali Akbar," described as "8th in line as a descendant of Hazrat Shamsuddin Sabzwari"; the official Punjab Archaeology page instead names the founder only as "the Ismaili Saint Sultan Ali Akbar," who "erected the tomb according to local tradition," without repeating the Shamsuddin Sabzwari descent claim. A third, less central discrepancy: the two Tribune articles report different conservation-project cost figures (Rs 30 million in May 2019 versus Rs 27.104 million in November 2019), which may represent the same project re-costed at tender stage or two different phases — not clarified by either article. Per the research verdict, this addition is treated as PARTIAL rather than STRONG: the two press articles may derive from the same government press-office material (near-identical phrasing across both), and given the direct conflict with the official custodial body on the central fact of construction date, this addition has not yet been independently corroborated to a settled standard.
